Monday, November 9, 2026

Space & Defense Daily — Monday, Nov 9, 2026

A new Democratic Congress looks set to rein in and likely rename Golden Dome, with space-based interceptors most at risk; NATO is about €7 billion short on its 2026 Ukraine aid pledge as Europe rehearses a postwar Ukraine force in Poland and heads to the Abu Dhabi talks; NASA launched CLPS 2, a $10 billion lunar lander contract with eight companies, plus a nuclear-powered rover and about $1.3 billion in transport task orders.

← NewerTue, Nov 10, 2026All briefingsOlder →Fri, Nov 6, 2026
NATOEuropean UnionUnited StatesEuropean spaceGlobal space & defense

Top stories: Ars Technica reports that, with Golden Dome's congressional champions leaving and Democrats taking the gavels in January, the program faces real budget scrutiny, a likely new name, and probable cuts to space-based interceptors, while Breaking Defense says reconciliation and FY27 appropriations look unlikely in the lame duck. Politico reports NATO allies are about €7 billion short of the €70 billion Ukraine military-aid pledge for 2026, as 2,800 troops from 11 nations start the KOALICJA 26.2 exercise in Poland to rehearse a postwar Multinational Force-Ukraine and Europe says it will be at the table for the Nov. 10–11 U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. And NASA picked eight companies for CLPS 2, a 10-year lunar delivery contract worth up to $10 billion, alongside the nuclear-powered PROMISE rover and about $1.3 billion in VADR launch and orbital-transfer task orders.

NATO

  • NATO allies face a roughly €7 billion gap on the €70 billion in military aid they pledged to Ukraine for 2026, including a $1.9 billion hole in unpaid PURL deliveries of U.S. weapons, ahead of a Nov. 17 alliance meeting on boosting funding and air-defense transfers. (Politico Europe)
  • The UK and France lead KOALICJA 26.2 from Nov. 9 to 22, bringing 2,800 troops from 11 nations to Poland, France and Turkey to rehearse how the Coalition of the Willing's Multinational Force-Ukraine would move, protect and supply itself after a ceasefire; the force would not be under NATO command and U.S. troops are not taking part. (Defense News)
  • Romania scrambled two Spanish F-18s flying NATO's eastern-flank air policing mission from Mihail Kogălniceanu on Nov. 8 after radar spotted two unidentified targets near Ukraine's Snake Island, and issued an RO-Alert warning in Tulcea County; there was no confirmed violation of Romanian airspace. (Kyiv24)

European Union

  • France's foreign minister said Europeans will be "well represented" at the U.S.-brokered Abu Dhabi talks on Nov. 10–11, though the EU is still sorting out who speaks for it; António Costa has put the question on the agenda of the Nov. 13 leaders' summit, and Kaja Kallas said "Putin does not have a veto over European security." (Politico Europe)
  • Rheinmetall cut its 2026 sales outlook to about €13.2 billion despite 36% Q3 sales growth, because Germany's Arminius Boxer contract has slipped to Q1 2027 and artillery-ammunition acceptance tests are running long; its backlog stands at €78 billion and it has started handing over XM30 prototypes to the U.S. Army. (Defense World)
  • EU Defence and Space Commissioner Andrius Kubilius visited Sweden on Nov. 5–6, touring KTH's Swedish Gunpowder nitrocellulose centre and SSC's Esrange Space Center in Kiruna with Defence Minister Pål Jonson. (Nordic Defence Sector)

United States

  • Ars Technica reports that seven Golden Dome Caucus members, including co-chair Jeff Crank and Strategic Forces chair Scott DesJarlais, are leaving Congress; sources expect Democrats to cap funding, likely rename the program, and cut space-based interceptors, while the FY27 request of more than $17 billion was mostly tied to a stalled $350 billion reconciliation package. (Ars Technica)
  • Analysts tell Breaking Defense that reconciliation and FY27 defense appropriations are unlikely to pass in the five-week lame duck, with a roughly $1.1 trillion topline more likely than $1.5 trillion, a possible shutdown after the Dec. 11 continuing resolution expires, and a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Hegseth expected. (Breaking Defense)
  • NASA picked Blue Origin, Firefly, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX and Voyager for CLPS 2, a 10-year contract worth up to $10 billion. It also raised CLPS 1 to $4.2 billion, moved ahead with the nuclear-powered PROMISE rover for late 2028 (Blue Origin delivers it for $94 million), and issued about $1.3 billion in VADR task orders plus a Starship cislunar comms demo. (NASA)
  • SpaceX launched the classified USSF-432 (R-4) mission on Falcon 9 from Vandenberg at 4:48 p.m. PT on Nov. 6; the previous R launches each put 23 satellites, believed to be Starshield-based, into orbit for the Space-Based Sensing and Targeting program. (Spaceflight Now)
  • Next up, SpaceX is targeting tonight, Nov. 9, at 7:07 p.m. PT for the USSF-627 Falcon 9 launch from Vandenberg SLC-4E, with a backup on Nov. 10. (SpaceX)
  • SciTec, a Firefly company, has added data from Space Systems Command's Wide Field of View satellite in geostationary orbit to the Space Force's FORGE missile-warning ground system under its $259 million FORGE EOS contract. (SatNow)
  • AST SpaceMobile will support prime contractor STR on a new phase of a U.S. Space Force contract to develop space-based sensing using its BlueBird phased-array technology. (SatNow)
  • A White House "declaration" on American freedom in space, unveiled around President Trump's Nov. 6 visit to Kennedy Space Center, mostly restates existing policy and law, drawing reactions from dismissal to cautious support. (SpaceNews)
  • Air & Space Forces Magazine looks at how the Space Force is studying very low Earth orbit operations as commercial firms and researchers push satellites to lower altitudes. (Air & Space Forces Magazine)

European space

  • ESA's Hera released its final-approach sequence to the Didymos–Dimorphos asteroid pair after October braking burns, and says detailed images of the DART impact target will be unveiled on Nov. 25. (ESA)
  • ESA's reusable methane Prometheus engine made its first hot-fire at DLR's upgraded P5 bench in Lampoldshausen. It used a cold-gas-spray combustion chamber and reignited several times without a high-pressure starter, which ESA calls a European first for an engine of its class. (ESA)
  • Thales Alenia Space gave MDA Space an authorization to proceed worth more than $100 million for AURORA digital phased-array antennas and controllers on the 66 Layer 1 IRIS² satellites, which are due in 2029. (Electronics Weekly)

Global space & defense

  • Ukraine's military intelligence told Reuters that Russia is already using its Rassvet satellite network, a homegrown Starlink rival, for intermittent military communications over Ukraine to make strike drones more accurate and harder to jam; 32 satellites are up, and Bureau 1440 is targeting more than 900 by 2035. (Reuters)
  • Russia fired 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, including North Korean KN-23s, overnight into Nov. 7, blacking out five regions; Zelenskyy said Moscow is trying to pressure Kyiv before the Abu Dhabi talks and pressed the U.S. for Patriot interceptors. (The Guardian)
  • Russia said its overnight strikes into Nov. 8 hit three cargo ships near Odesa and Chornomorsk that it claimed were carrying military goods, plus two substations; DTEK said more than 600,000 people in Dnipropetrovsk lost power. Reuters could not verify the ship claims. (The Moscow Times / Reuters)
  • China launched the 29th group of its state-owned Guowang low-orbit internet satellites on a Long March 12 from Wenchang early Nov. 9 Beijing time, which was China's 82nd launch of 2026. (China Daily)
  • In a four-launch week for China, the Ceres-2 and Kinetica-2 commercial rockets both reached orbit on their second flights, and Kinetica-2 carried Qianfan constellation satellites. (SpaceNews)
